idiom_name: Map keyed by position (one per rule) + has()-based memo wrapper
implementation_notes: A rule is an ordinary function of the input position, so the whole pattern is a Map per rule (or one Map on a composite key) plus a three-line wrapper: read the cache, compute on a miss, store the result - success and failure - so re-entering the same rule at the same offset returns the cached outcome. What replaces the classic memo-table structure is that no table object exists: the Map is a closure variable and the hit test is has(), because get() returns undefined both for a missing key and for a rule that legitimately produced nothing. Peggy ships the same trade-off as a generation option (--cache), documented as avoiding exponential parse time in pathological cases while making the parser slower - which is why it is off by default.
pitfalls: get() returning undefined conflates 'not computed' with 'computed and produced nothing': use has(), or make every stored result an object.
A module-level cache outlives the parse - it keeps the previous tree alive and answers from stale offsets when the next input differs; scope the Map to one parse and clear it.
The table is sized by the input: one entry per rule and position costs far more than the input itself, so long-lived parsers must cap, shard or drop it.
